name: Questions, Groups, and the Teacher's First Call
title: Questions, Groups, and the Teacher's First Call
answer: AI can draft comprehension questions at several levels and suggest reading groups from assessment data, but the teacher must review the questions and form their own groups before comparing them with the tool's suggestion. This matters because group placement shapes what a child reads for weeks, and the teacher holds knowledge the data may miss.

crumbs.name: Reading and Writing, Kindergarten Through 12th Grade

sections.body: This idea covers two uses of AI in reading and writing instruction: drafting comprehension questions and suggesting reading groups. Teachers spend a great deal of time writing questions about texts, and AI tools can produce questions ranging from simple recall to inference and analysis, which tools such as Google Forms can turn into quick checks. The teacher then reviews the questions for accuracy and removes any that could be answered without reading the text. A good question bank saves hours and lets teachers check understanding more often. Assessment results can also shape reading groups, with a screener or practice platform suggesting which students belong together for guided reading.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In the classroom, the teacher uses AI-drafted questions as a starting point, checking each one for accuracy and discarding any that a student could answer without having read the text, then turning the kept questions into quick checks through a tool such as Google Forms. For grouping, the teacher forms their own reading groups first, based on what they know about each student, and only then compares those groups with the tool's suggestion. Where the two differ, the teacher looks closer at the individual student. The teacher's judgment decides the final placement. The text does not give separate grade band guidance for this idea.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text cites research on human review for a specific order of work: the teacher should form their own groups first, then compare them with the tool's suggestion (Krugel et al., 2023). Where the two differ, the teacher looks closer, and the teacher's judgment decides. The text offers no other study, figure or finding for this idea.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The order of work is the main safeguard: the teacher forms groups first and treats the tool's suggestion as a second opinion, so the teacher's knowledge stays in the decision. This matters because group placement shapes what a child reads for weeks. A tool's suggestion is based only on the data it has, which may miss a child who tested badly on a hard day or who reads far better than they write. The teacher knows those things, and the teacher's judgment decides where students are placed.
